styleAnswer.evidence: The piano is a small, boxy, almost frontal object. Its dark cabinet has only about 3-4 lightness steps: a body tone, a slightly lighter top panel, a dark keyboard strip and a few white or black key pixels. There is no wood grain, no edge highlight and no side or top bevel to model the cabinet. Measured facts: 11 visible tones per tile and 4% near-flat coverage, with 0% neutral dark edges, so the outline is tinted rather than a black sticker line. That is on par with prop-hedge (9 tones) but well below prop-well-roofed (20) and prop-stall-cheese (17), the richer references, which show per-material ramps, grain and individually shaded parts. By eye, the candidate reads as a flat dark slab with a keyboard pasted on. It is thinner and flatter than the Beodeul pieces, and the cabinet lacks the texture dots and tonal variety they carry. Doubt resolves to fail.

styleAnswer.evidence: The upright piano has a dark body with a lighter lid edge, a grey music-stand panel with a small logo, and a keyboard with white and black keys, so it reads as modelled and not as a sticker. Its dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the outline leans toward the body's own dark tone and is not a uniform black line. It shows 11 visible tones per 16x16 tile, above the hedge (9) and below the stall (17) and well (20). Near-flat coverage is 4%, close to the stall's 13% and far from a flat fill. The weak spot is the large dark body, which carries only about 4 lightness steps and little grain compared with the stall roof or well. Because a black instrument naturally uses a narrow value range, and the measured facts sit within the reference range, this is slightly lower than the best references but acceptable.
